bib.title: Lessons from the Trenches on Reproducible Evaluation of Language Models

read.skipped: Reference list (offsets ~43398-121425) skimmed only for lineage, not read line by line.

question: What practical challenges make language model evaluation hard to reproduce and compare, and which practices (as built into lm-eval) mitigate them?
hypothesis: Minor implementation details such as prompt format, scoring and averaging choices strongly change scores and rankings, so undisclosed setups make results irreproducible.
contributions: Collect and present common challenges in LM evaluation with concrete instances
Document how the practices are operationalized in lm-eval

method.summary: Experience report from the lm-eval developers plus one small case study: 5 pretrained LMs are scored 0-shot on ARC-Challenge (cloze vs MMLU-style prompt) and MMLU (Hybrid vs MMLU-style prompt) with lm-eval v0.4.2. The rest is prose recommendations, formal definitions of loglikelihood, perplexity and generative scoring (App B), and a checklist (App D).
method.task: multiple-choice QA evaluation sensitivity to prompt format

datasets.name: ARC-Challenge
datasets.preprocessing: cloze: 'Question: {question}\nAnswer:' scored over answer texts; MMLU-style: question plus lettered choices, scored over letters

datasets.name: MMLU
datasets.preprocessing: MMLU-style scores letters A-D; Hybrid uses the same prompt but scores the answer strings

datasets.name: ARC-Easy
datasets.preprocessing: cloze vs MMLU-style; only GPT-NeoX-20B numbers quoted in text

inference.decoding: loglikelihood ranking over answer choices, no sampling
inference.samples: single pass per model and setting; 95% bootstrap CI over questions
inference.prompting: 0-shot as stated in Table 1 caption; two prompt styles per benchmark

parameters.metric: acc (unnormalized loglikelihood); acc_norm is byte-length normalised

metrics.name: acc
metrics.definition: fraction of items where the choice with highest (unnormalized) conditional loglikelihood is correct; MMLU is micro-averaged over documents

baselines: cloze vs MMLU-style vs Hybrid prompt styles
eval.protocol: Bootstrapped standard errors reported as +/- (checklist says 95% CIs); single run; no significance tests between styles.

availability.code: https://github.com/EleutherAI/lm-evaluation-harness/tree/v0.4.2/lm_eval; YAML configs for the case study printed in Appendix C.1

prompts.purpose: ARC cloze prompt (Brown et al. 2020 style)

evidence.quote: All experiments are run on 8x NVIDIA A40 48Gb GPUs. Total usage time did not exceed 1 day.

results.claim: Prompt style changes 0-shot accuracy by more than 20 points in some cases, and the best style varies by model.
results.setup: 0-shot, ARC-Challenge (cloze vs MMLU-style) and MMLU (Hybrid vs MMLU-style), five pretrained LMs, lm-eval v0.4.2
results.quote: performance varies dramatically with the prompt (in some cases, > 20%), and which prompt style works best varies by model

results.claim: Mixtral-8x7B ARC-Challenge accuracy: cloze 56.7 vs MMLU-style 81.3.
results.setup: 0-shot, lm-eval v0.4.2; 95% bootstrap CI 2.23 on MMLU-style
results.table: Table 1, row Mixtral-8x7B, columns ARC (Challenge) Cloze / MMLU-style
Table 1, row Mistral-7B, columns ARC (Challenge) Cloze / MMLU-style

results.claim: GPT-NeoX-20B and Falcon-7B fall to about chance on ARC-Challenge under MMLU-style (26.6, 25.9) but score 38.0 and 40.2 with cloze.
results.table: Table 1, rows GPT-NeoX-20B and Falcon-7B, column ARC (Challenge) MMLU-style

results.claim: On MMLU, Mixtral-8x7B scores 67.1 with the original MMLU-style prompt vs 59.7 with the Hybrid prompt.
results.note: Llama-2-7B: Hybrid 39.8, MMLU-style 41.3; GPT-NeoX-20B: Hybrid 27.6, MMLU-style 24.5, so the better style differs by model
results.table: Table 1, row Mixtral-8x7B, columns MMLU Hybrid / MMLU-style

results.claim: GPT-NeoX-20B on ARC-Easy: 72.4 cloze vs 26.5 MMLU-style.
results.quote: using the “cloze” evaluation setup, GPT-NeoX achieves an accuracy of 72.4 ± 1.80% but using the MMLU-style setup it scores 26.5 ± 1.78%

results.claim: Model-failure to follow the MMLU-style output format, not lack of knowledge, explains chance scores for GPT-NeoX-20B.
results.quote: this at-random performance is a result of failing to follow the task and output format for this prompting style, even when it can score well using an alternative format

results.claim: Three MMLU implementations (HELM, lm-eval, original code) give widely different scores and change model rankings.
results.quote: comparing three independent implementations of MMLU (HELM, lm-eval, and the original MMLU code), they find that these implementations produce widely different scores and even change the ranking order of models

results.claim: Single-run point estimates on GPQA give a different picture than a 95% CI over 10 runs.
results.setup: GPQA, OpenAI and Anthropic models, 10 runs
results.quote: Presenting single-run point estimates of performance (top) instead of a 95% confidence interval across 10 runs of the benchmark (bottom) paints a very different pictures

results.claim: MMLU micro vs macro averaging across 57 subjects changes results by several percentage points.
results.setup: MMLU; no numbers or model given
results.quote: the choice of which affects results by several percentage points

results.claim: lm-eval reports bootstrapped standard errors by default; these measure question-sampling variation, not run-to-run stochasticity.
results.quote: We report bootstrapped standard error metrics by default

results.claim: Open LLM Leaderboard users fine-tuned to match the eval format (e.g. separator tokens), an instance of the Benchmark Lottery.
results.quote: practitioners have been observed fine-tuning their models specifically to match the evaluation format used by the leaderboard

results.claim: Fixed-length non-overlapping windows for perplexity skew results toward longer-context models (Early Token Curse).
results.setup: perplexity on sequences longer than context
results.quote: systematically skews results in favor of models trained and thus evaluated with longer context lengths

results.claim: Multiple-choice loglikelihood benchmarks do not agree with generative-scored multiple-choice benchmarks.
results.quote: multiple-choice loglikelihood-based benchmarks do not even agree with generative-scored multiple-choice benchmarks

results.claim: Frames the Key Problem: the best tools for judging semantic equivalence are the models being evaluated; responses are closed-domain conversion, model-based grading, or human labor.
results.quote: our best automated tools for determining whether two sentences are semantically equivalent are the very models we are seeking to evaluate

limits: Scope is MCQA only; the authors say they focus on it because it is the approach they know best and urge experts in other approaches to document theirs.
Limitations appendix (F) is truncated mid-sentence and says measurement validity is not discussed in detail.
Case study uses five base models, one lm-eval version and two prompt styles per benchmark; no per-run variance and no significance test between styles.
Model-based grading (LLM-as-judge) is only mentioned as flawed, with citations; no judge experiments are run.
Authors infer that Mistral and Llama reports used MMLU-style prompts for ARC; this is a belief, not confirmed.
Conventions date quickly (Sec 2.3), so recommendations may age.
practices: Report full prompts and detail methodology, including prompt-engineering effort, loglikelihood and generation hyperparameters and answer extraction heuristics (Sec 3.2, App D).
Do not copy results from other papers unless the same code was used (App D).
Provide model outputs so scores can be recomputed (App D).
Report variance and statistical significance rather than point estimates (Sec 4.2, App D).
Evaluate in realistic settings and do qualitative error analysis before scaling (Sec 4.2, App D).
Prefer procedures agreed by LLM trainers, then official implementations, then evaluator consensus (Sec 3.3 priority list).
Log per-sample outputs and dry-run with --limit and --log_samples (Sec 3.3).

terms.definition: there can be many semantically equivalent but syntactically different ways of expressing the same idea, and the best tools to detect equivalence are the models being evaluated
popular benchmarks can have a distorting effect on the field, redefining success in ways that reinforce their particular idiosyncrasies and even flaws
an MMLU-style prompt but using the answer strings instead of answer letters as the set of continuations scored
tokens with more preceding context are easier to predict, skewing non-overlapping-window perplexity
